units.title: Unit 15 — Marketing
learningObjectives: Identify and use natural collocations for market research, demographic profiles and purchasing behaviour.
Distinguish connected expressions for segmentation, customers, brand identity and market share.
Describe campaigns, advertising channels and promotional exposure with appropriate register.
Explain customer satisfaction, loyalty and brand-awareness goals using accurate word partnerships.

items.example: The subscription service interviewed its target customers before changing the price.
items.note: Target customers are the specific buyers a product or service aims to attract.

items.example: Changing consumer demands prompted the company to redesign its packaging.
items.note: Demands refers to what consumers require or expect from products.

items.example: The survey revealed consumer preferences for smaller containers.
items.note: Preferences identifies what buyers or users favour among available options.

items.example: Before opening the café, the owners will conduct market research locally.
items.note: Conduct or carry out market research is idiomatic; make market research is not.

items.example: The retailer hired a specialist to carry out market research in three cities.
items.note: Carry out and conduct are both natural verbs with market research.

items.pt: grupo focal; grupo de discussão de consumidores
items.example: A focus group examined three possible designs for the new logo.
items.note: A focus group brings selected people together to discuss their reactions to a product or idea.

items.example: The analysts monitored consumer behaviour during the holiday season.
items.note: Behaviour covers how consumers choose, use and respond to products.

items.example: The loyalty data showed that buying habits changed after the store moved online.
items.note: Buying habits are repeated patterns of purchasing rather than a single transaction.

items.example: The new model is priced for households in a lower income bracket.
items.note: An income bracket is a category based on earnings; higher and lower are common modifiers.

items.example: A demographic profile helped the team identify the average customer age.
items.note: This profile summarises customer characteristics such as age and occupation.

items.pt: gestão do relacionamento com o cliente
items.example: Better customer relationship management improved the handling of repeat enquiries.
items.note: Often abbreviated to CRM; it concerns how an organisation manages interactions with customers.

items.example: The airline redesigned its booking process to improve the customer experience.
items.note: Customer experience covers the overall interaction with a company, not only satisfaction.

items.example: Clear renewal reminders helped the service improve customer retention.
items.note: Customer retention means keeping existing customers over time.

items.example: The new delivery policy should better match customer expectations.
items.note: Customer expectations are what people anticipate from a product or service.

items.example: The design team prioritised customer needs over decorative features.
items.note: Customer needs describes what purchasers require; it contrasts with optional preferences.

items.example: Feedback from early users shaped product development throughout the spring.
items.note: Product development covers creating or improving a product before or during release.

items.example: The company changed its product design to make repairs easier.
items.note: Product design deals with the form, function and usability of an offering.

items.example: Market segmentation helped the publisher offer different subscriptions to students and firms.
items.note: Market segmentation divides potential consumers into groups with shared characteristics.

items.example: The competitor gained market share despite selling fewer product lines.
items.note: Market share is the proportion of total sales held by one company or brand.

items.example: The marketing campaign introduced the service to first-time buyers.
items.note: A marketing campaign is a coordinated series of actions intended to promote an offering.

items.example: The museum chose young families as the target audience for its weekend events.
items.note: The target audience is the particular group a campaign is designed to reach.

items.example: Short videos helped the charity reach the target audience more effectively.
items.note: Reach pairs with an audience to describe successful exposure to a message.

items.pt: direcionar ações a um segmento de mercado
items.example: The startup plans to target a market segment that values repairable devices.
items.note: Target is a verb for focusing an offer or campaign on a specific group.

items.example: The festival used billboard advertising near the railway station.
items.note: Billboard advertising places promotional messages on large outdoor displays.

items.example: The drama included product placement for several familiar electronics brands.
items.note: Product placement puts a branded item within entertainment content, often for payment.

items.example: A street installation became the centre of a guerrilla marketing campaign.
items.note: Guerrilla marketing uses unconventional attention-grabbing tactics, often at low cost.

items.example: The in-house marketing team prepared the launch without using outside designers.
items.note: In-house means employed within the organisation, as opposed to an external agency.

items.example: An advertising agency developed the visuals for the regional campaign.
items.note: An advertising agency is an external specialist organisation that creates promotions.

items.example: Consistent typography gives the retailer a recognisable brand identity.
items.note: Brand identity means how a business intends its brand to be recognised.

items.example: The campaign increased brand awareness among people who had never heard of the product.
items.note: Brand awareness means that potential customers know a brand exists.

items.pt: aumentar o conhecimento sobre uma marca
items.example: The sports club hopes to build brand awareness through community events.
items.note: Build brand awareness is an established verb-noun pairing for increasing familiarity.

items.example: A shorter waiting time improved customer satisfaction in the survey.
items.note: Customer satisfaction measures how happy buyers are with goods or service.

items.example: The points programme was designed to encourage customer loyalty.
items.note: Customer loyalty describes repeated commitment to a brand or business.

items.example: A short demonstration video went viral after a popular creator shared it.
items.note: Go viral means spread rapidly through online sharing; viral is not a paid-advertising channel.

items.example: The team answered questions about the new product on social media.
items.note: Social media is the collective term for online sharing and interaction platforms.

items.pt: tempo de exposição gratuito na mídia
items.example: An unexpected television interview gave the project valuable free airtime.
items.note: Free airtime is broadcast exposure obtained without paying for advertising.

items.example: The opening of the new centre attracted favourable press coverage.
items.note: Press coverage is news reporting, as distinct from advertising purchased by a firm.

items.example: The cosmetics brand secured celebrity endorsement for its new range.
items.note: Celebrity endorsement uses a famous person to publicly promote a product.

items.example: The shop uses live demonstrations to engage with customers directly.
items.note: Engage with customers implies active two-way interaction, not just showing an advert.

items.section: Practice · Brand and market word families
items.example: The distinctive symbol improved brand recognition across different countries.
items.note: Brand recognition is identifying a particular brand when presented with its cues.

items.section: Practice · Brand and market word families
items.example: The company registered a new brand name before entering the market.
items.note: A brand name is the verbal identity under which products are sold.

items.section: Practice · Brand and market word families
items.example: The supplier became the market leader in affordable water filters.
items.note: A market leader holds a leading competitive position in its market.

items.section: Practice · Brand and market word families
items.example: The marketing plan considered each stage of the product life cycle.
items.note: This term describes the stages from introduction to eventual decline or withdrawal.

items.section: Practice · Brand and market word families
items.example: Managers praised the service team for maintaining a strong customer focus.
items.note: Customer focus means putting customer needs at the centre of decisions.

items.section: Practice · Brand and market word families
items.example: A market survey tested demand before the company expanded into the region.
items.note: Market survey normally refers to collecting information from potential buyers.

units.title: Unit 16 — Customer services
learningObjectives: Describe shopping choices, product suitability, value and customer satisfaction in idiomatic English.
Understand customer complaints, slow deliveries, refunds and service recovery using precise expressions.
Distinguish informal protest language from formal customer-service commitments and responses.
Use the correct grammatical partners and prepositions with order, complaint, conform and standard.

items.example: The supermarket will carry out surveys to identify problems with its delivery service.
items.note: Carry out or do surveys is normal; make surveys is not the expected collocation.

items.example: The cinema decided to do a customer survey after renovating the building.
items.note: Do a survey is natural English and refers to systematic feedback collection.

items.example: Online shopping is convenient for people who cannot visit a store.
items.note: Online shopping is the standard phrase, rather than on-the-web shopping.

items.example: We usually go shopping on Saturday mornings when the market opens.
items.note: Go shopping is idiomatic; make shopping is not used for this activity.

items.pt: na rua comercial principal; no comércio local
items.example: Several independent shops on the high street now offer home delivery.
items.note: Mainly British English for the principal street with shops in a town.

items.example: The basic subscription offers better value for money than the premium plan.
items.note: Value for money concerns whether the benefits justify the price, not just cheapness.

items.pt: adequado à finalidade; próprio para uso
items.example: The replacement scanner must be fit for purpose in a busy laboratory.
items.note: Fit for purpose means suitable for the intended practical use.

items.example: The passenger decided to make a complaint about the cancellation.
items.note: Make a complaint is the natural verb-noun combination; complaint is a noun.

items.example: The retailer will offer a discount to subscribers renewing early.
items.note: Offer a discount means propose a price reduction to the purchaser.

items.example: You can place an order through the app until midnight.
items.note: Place an order is standard in commerce; put an order is not idiomatic.

items.example: Regular customers receive advance notice of seasonal promotions.
items.note: Regular customers return frequently; this does not necessarily mean they are satisfied.

items.example: The restaurant invited satisfied customers to share feedback online.
items.note: Satisfied modifies customers whose expectations have been met, not satisfactory customers.

items.example: Healthy competition encouraged both shops to improve their service.
items.note: Healthy competition means rivalry that benefits the market and consumers.

items.pt: uma pesquisa de grande escala com clientes
items.example: The company commissioned a large-scale customer survey across six regions.
items.note: Large-scale specifies the broad extent of a survey; customer identifies respondents.

items.example: Contactless payment has become increasingly popular in smaller shops.
items.note: Increasingly combines with an adjective to show a growing degree over time.

items.example: The repair company is known for prompt service after a fault is reported.
items.note: Prompt service means delivered quickly and without unnecessary delay.

items.example: The bookstore offered next-day delivery for orders placed before noon.
items.note: Next-day delivery specifies arrival on the following day; it is not a vague promise of speed.

items.pt: colocar alguém em espera no telefone
items.example: The support agent put me on hold while checking the invoice.
items.note: On hold describes waiting on a telephone call; hold is the necessary noun.

items.example: The team promised to get back to the customer by the afternoon.
items.note: Get back to someone means reply later with requested information.

items.example: The customer returned the headset because of its poor quality.
items.note: Poor quality is idiomatic for products that do not meet acceptable standards.

items.example: The workshop advertises top quality furniture made from reclaimed wood.
items.note: Top quality is a promotional phrase for especially good quality products.

items.pt: fazer um escândalo; reclamar com veemência
items.example: Several passengers kicked up a fuss when their luggage disappeared.
items.note: Informal and disapproving; means protest loudly or make a forceful complaint.

items.example: She decided to demand a full refund after the replacement also failed.
items.note: Demand is already forceful, so strongly demand adds an unnecessary intensifier.

items.pt: passar a comprar de outro fornecedor
items.example: After repeated delays, we chose to take our custom elsewhere.
items.note: Primarily British English; custom refers to a customer’s purchasing business.

items.example: A senior employee will handle the complaint before the weekend.
items.note: Handle a complaint is idiomatic for managing it through a resolution.

items.example: The recurring fault gave residents grounds for complaint.
items.note: Grounds is plural here and means a justified reason for complaining.

items.example: The company trains new employees to provide an excellent service.
items.note: Provide an excellent service is a formal promise of service quality.

items.pt: estar em conformidade com as normas de segurança
items.example: All imported chargers must conform to safety regulations.
items.note: Conform to is the required verb-preposition pattern for meeting regulations.

items.example: Suppliers are expected to honour commitments made in their contracts.
items.note: Honour commitments means fulfil what was promised, with British spelling honour.

items.example: The service manager assured clients that the firm would take complaints seriously.
items.note: Take seriously is the idiomatic structure; serious is an adjective, not an adverb here.

items.example: The inspection found that the repairs did not come up to standard.
items.note: Come up to standard means meet the acceptable quality threshold.

items.example: The provider pledged to handle complaints promptly in future.
items.note: Promptly modifies how efficiently and quickly complaints are resolved.

items.example: If the device fails again, the shop will offer a replacement.
items.note: Offer a replacement means provide an alternative item rather than simply refunding it.

items.example: The passenger received a full refund when the tour was cancelled.
items.note: A full refund returns the entire sum paid; partial refund returns only some.

items.example: Students receive a discount on books at the campus shop.
items.note: Discount normally takes on before the goods receiving the price reduction.

items.example: The latest safety regulations require stronger electrical insulation.
items.note: Regulations are formal requirements that organisations or products must obey.

items.example: Unfortunately, the replacement service did not come up to expectations.
items.note: The pattern come up to also combines with expectations or standard.

items.example: The warranty centre aims to provide prompt service even at busy times.
items.note: Provide takes a service as its object, while prompt describes timely delivery.

items.example: The company apologised publicly for poor service during the outage.
items.note: Poor is the ordinary adjective for unacceptable service quality.
